scores.evidence: The H2 heading leads with the verdict, but the opening paragraphs under it spend three sentences narrating context before delivering the mechanism claim
'The verdict' section explicitly restates the argument: 'Antonelli's win was earned on pace and unlocked by circumstance, in that order' — a textbook summary paragraph
'Behind the Mercedes one-two, Verstappen brought...' is a bridging sentence doing transitional work inside the evidence section rather than letting a heading carry it
3.857 seconds, 1:23.504, four tenths, 0.16, 0.90 — figures cluster in one paragraph rather than being deployed singly to clinch discrete claims
'finishing perhaps sixth' uses a hedge, but 'the result was only ever a matter of whether ten laps was enough' asserts certainty for a counterfactual without earned documentation
Russell is consistently the primary benchmark throughout: 'eight tenths per lap that George Russell could not answer,' 'pass his team-mate'
No quotes, radio messages, or official communications appear anywhere in the text despite the subject matter inviting them
'fourteenth on lap one became eighth by lap six' — recaps the running order rather than interpreting what the pace delta meant strategically
'Russell may quietly note that he led thirty of fifty-three laps and lost' approaches dry irony but the surrounding prose leans toward earnest analytical summary rather than juxtaposition
No first-person voice appears anywhere; the meta-framing ('analyst-pipeline pilot,' 'the recap treats them as reported rather than measured') substitutes institutional distancing for personality
'teams may change tyres at no time cost' explains the red-flag tyre rule — unnecessary for an enthusiast audience; otherwise jargon is handled well
Opening section under first H2 runs two paragraphs of 4-5 sentences each; the 'caveat' section contains one paragraph of seven sentences — both violate the 2-4 sentence rule
'It was, by one lap.' works as a short punch; but most paragraphs sustain uniform analytical sentence length without visible variation
Density does peak at the gap table mechanism, but the caveat section gives equal or greater room to secondary threads (Pérez penalty, Gasly pole) than their significance warrants

top_fixes: Delete 'The verdict' section entirely — S2 is a hard rule; the piece should end when the caveat section ends, letting Russell's muted afternoon serve as the coda
Insert at least two evidentiary quotes or radio messages (team-to-driver, Antonelli post-race, or stewards' document on the Pérez penalty) — E4 is scoring zero and dragging credibility

Add a first-person judgment call in one place where the analyst is genuinely speculating — the Gasly pole cause or the Hamilton contact adjudication are natural sites — to satisfy R3 and break the institutional-voice flatness that signals machine authorship most loudly

scores.evidence: 'A big early crash, back-and-forths up and down the field, and the late hunt for victory made this a lively Monza race'
'So, this was certainly one of those frustrating weekends' — soft closing sentence rather than a summary paragraph, but still a mild wrap-up coda
Sections open cleanly on their verdict, but bridging phrases like 'That's the debate The Race had when putting this list together' dissolve the abruptness
'the slight 3.8-second margin of victory' and '66 points ahead' appear in the same section; numbers cluster rather than each clinching a single claim
'May well have been', 'surely', 'certainly' used, but 'surely there's no stopping this title charge now' passes off speculation as near-certainty without an explicit marker
Norris/Piastri framing gestures at teammate benchmark but Lawson, Hamilton, Russell sections skip it in favour of absolute comparisons
Hamilton's 'here there are no rules' quote and Russell's tyre-strategy quote both land as hard stops that complicate or confirm the preceding reading
'Starting from the pitlane in the aftermath of power unit changes necessitated by the battery issue in Q1' — recaps context the reader watched rather than interpreting it
'the only way the badly outmatched AMR26s were ever going to influence things' is dry, but 'sky is falling down' is rhetorical flourish rather than earned understatement
'this writer specifically' flags a judgment call correctly, but 'Here's our pick of winners and losers from race day in Italy' is a sentence about the piece itself
No definitions offered for VSC, ICoA context, DRS; Parabolica, Lesmo 2 named without orientation — peer address maintained throughout
Ferrari section has a five-sentence paragraph beginning 'Whatever the inside-team ruling' that bundles three separate points without exiting

'He was also gracious in defeat, taking nothing away from Antonelli's recovery to victory, and paying little attention to the podium boos - but the reality is now stark: Antonelli is 66 points ahead and going strong' — long sentence, punchy follow-through, but this rhythm is intermittent
Ferrari (the big story) gets room; Racing Bulls gets comparable length; Verstappen (clear-cut positive) runs four paragraphs when two would do

top_fixes: Kill the intro blurb ('A big early crash… Here's our pick') entirely — open on Antonelli's verdict without scene-setting; the bylines and subheads do all the structural work needed.
Enforce one number per claim: strip the Russell section to either the 3.8-second gap or the 66-point deficit, not both; use the survivor to clinch a single sharp point.

Close Verstappen and Lawson two sentences earlier each — both sections drift into soft summary ('how good was it to see', 'certainly one of those frustrating weekends') that pads clear-cut verdicts beyond their weight.

scores.evidence: 'With 15 minutes to go before qualifying at Monza, pole contender George Russell revealed' — narrative scene-setting, verdict buried or absent
'The lengthy saga has cost Gasly and Alpine nine points...while also raising questions' — classic wrap-up synthesis restating the argument
'It was the scene of his first and so far only victory...and now he has grabbed his first pole' — bridging sentence connecting sections rather than abrupt heading transition
'0.060s faster than Russell' and '0.001s' and '77cm' and '3mm' — figures deployed but clustered across passages rather than singly surgical
'This likely arose due to the addition of the Cadillac garage' — one hedged speculation, but most speculative claims lack explicit markers
Russell's performance never benchmarked against Antonelli; Piastri never against Norris; teammate comparison absent throughout
'Max was very clever there...that cost us both' — Wolff quote lands directly after the mechanical account of what Verstappen did, complicating the reading
'Russell was in a pack of cars led by Max Verstappen, who messed up his braking at Turn 1' — pure sequence narration of visible on-screen action
'less power than a Fiat Punto' is dry but borrowed from Verstappen; the piece's own prose is earnest rather than ironic
No first-person judgment calls appear; also two 'Thanks for reading F1 Debrief! Subscribe' sentences — explicit self-reference about the piece itself
'FIA International Court of Appeal (ICA)' — acronym spelled out; 'One Drop Foundation' context over-explained for an enthusiast audience
'Although FOM used LIDAR scans accurate to 3mm, it did not accurately reconstruct...as is usual post-race' — several paragraphs run to 5+ sentences
Some variation present ('That forced Antonelli to slow. That cost us both') but many paragraphs run in uniform mid-length sentences without punchy exits
ICA ruling gets extensive room, qualifying mechanism compressed; density inversion — procedural legalese expands while the actual lap mechanism stays thin

top_fixes: Invert every section opener: lead with the sharpest verdict ('Gasly's battery deployment was the story of qualifying; everything else was context'), then supply evidence — the chess anecdote and scene-setting are killing S1 throughout.

Cut both 'Thanks for reading' subscription plugs and the closing synthesis paragraph; the ICA statement is a fine hard stop — let it land without the 'nine points and questions raised' coda that re-narrates what the reader just processed.

Add one teammate benchmark per driver assessed: Antonelli's sector splits versus Russell, Norris versus Piastri at Turn 1 — without E3 anchors, individual verdicts float and the analysis reads as colour writing rather than evaluation.
